stem: Which bacteria live in the root nodules of soya beans and fix nitrogen?

options.content: *Rhizobium*
options.rationale: Correct: the nodule bacteria of legumes.

options.content: *Azotobacter*
options.rationale: A free-living nitrogen fixer, not a nodule bacterium.

options.content: *Nitrosomonas*
options.rationale: A nitrifying bacterium that turns ammonium into nitrite.

options.content: *Aspergillus*
options.rationale: A mould; one species produces aflatoxin.

explanation: *Rhizobium* (for soya, *Bradyrhizobium*) bacteria in nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen for the plant.

stem: Why is gypsum applied to groundnuts at early flowering?

options.content: To supply calcium for pod filling in the pegging zone
options.rationale: Correct: pods absorb calcium directly from the soil.

options.content: To supply nitrogen to the young leaves
options.rationale: Gypsum is calcium sulfate; it has no nitrogen.

options.content: To raise the soil pH strongly
options.rationale: Gypsum is nearly neutral; lime raises pH.

options.content: To kill the aphids that spread groundnut rosette virus
options.rationale: Gypsum is not an insecticide.

explanation: Without calcium in the pegging zone many pods are empty (pops).

stem: Why do groundnuts grow best on light, sandy loam soils?

options.content: Sandy soils always contain more nitrogen than clay soils do
options.rationale: Sandy soils are usually poorer in nutrients.

options.content: Pegs enter the soil easily and the pods lift out cleanly
options.rationale: Correct: heavy clay hinders pegging and harvest.

options.content: Groundnuts need waterlogged conditions
options.rationale: Groundnuts need well-drained soil.

options.content: Sandy soils hold far more water than clays
options.rationale: Clays hold more water than sands.

explanation: Pods develop underground, so a loose, well-drained soil suits pegging and lifting.

stem: Nyasha mixed soya seed with inoculant in full sun at 10:00 and planted it the next morning. What is the most likely result?

options.content: The seed fails to germinate at all
options.rationale: Inoculant does not affect germination.

options.content: Few nodules form because the bacteria died
options.rationale: Correct: sunlight, heat and delay kill Rhizobium.

options.content: The plants will form nodules but no pods
options.rationale: Pod formation is not prevented by this mistake.

options.content: The crop becomes resistant to soya bean rust
options.rationale: Inoculation has no effect on rust.

explanation: Inoculate in the shade and plant the same day; dead bacteria cannot form nodules, so the crop runs short of nitrogen.

stem: Why are groundnuts dried with the pods facing upwards, off the damp ground?

options.content: To let the pods continue to fill with oil after lifting
options.rationale: Pods do not fill after lifting.

options.content: To make the kernels sprout before storage
options.rationale: Sprouting spoils groundnuts.

options.content: To let rain wash soil off the shells
options.rationale: Wet pods mould; rain is avoided.

options.content: To prevent the mould that produces aflatoxin
options.rationale: Correct: quick drying stops Aspergillus mould growing.

explanation: Damp pods grow *Aspergillus* mould, which produces aflatoxin, a poison for people and livestock.

stem: Which insect spreads groundnut rosette virus?

options.content: Leafhoppers
options.rationale: Leafhoppers spread maize streak virus.

options.content: Bean fly
options.rationale: The bean fly maggot damages bean stems.

options.content: Bruchids
options.rationale: Bruchids attack stored beans.

options.content: Aphids
options.rationale: Correct: aphids carry the virus from plant to plant.

explanation: Early planting at a full, even stand reduces rosette, because aphids prefer sparse, late crops.

stem: Why should soya beans be harvested as soon as the pods are dry?

options.content: Dry soya seed loses all its oil within days
options.rationale: Oil content does not fall like this.

options.content: The plants regrow leaves and use up the seed
options.rationale: Mature soya does not regrow.

options.content: The pods turn into nodules
options.rationale: Pods and nodules are unrelated.

options.content: Dry pods shatter and drop their seed if left
options.rationale: Correct: delay causes heavy losses on the ground.

explanation: Shattering is the main harvest loss in soya, so cut and thresh promptly.
hints: What happens to very dry pods in hot weather?

stem: A farmer gave his soya crop a large nitrogen top dressing. Which result is most likely?

options.content: A doubling of yield, as soya cannot fix nitrogen
options.rationale: Well-nodulated soya fixes most of its own nitrogen.

options.content: Much more nodule growth on the roots of every single plant in the crop
options.rationale: Soil nitrate suppresses nodulation.

options.content: Little extra yield, since nodules fix less when nitrogen is plentiful
options.rationale: Correct: the money is largely wasted.

options.content: Protection of the crop from pod-sucking bugs
options.rationale: Nitrogen does not control insects.

explanation: Legumes need phosphorus and potassium; heavy nitrogen reduces fixation and seldom pays.
hints: Do nodules form more or less when the soil is rich in nitrate?

stem: Groundnut pods develop underground from pegs that grow down from fertilised flowers.
explanation: True. This is pegging; finish weeding before it starts so that pegs are not damaged.

stem: Soya beans grown on land that has never carried soya need no inoculation because all soils contain the right bacteria.
explanation: False. The specific bacteria for soya are usually absent from new land, so seed must be inoculated.

stem: Match each problem with the legume crop and cause.

right.content: Fly larva tunnelling in young bean stems

explanation: Know the main pests, diseases and disorders of each legume.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Gypsum is the chemical calcium {{blank:a}}; it supplies {{blank:b}} to groundnut pods.

explanation: Gypsum, calcium sulfate, supplies calcium (and sulfur) without raising pH much.

stem: Gypsum is spread at 300 kg/ha on 1.4 ha of groundnuts. How many 50 kg bags are needed? Round UP to whole bags.
explanation: 300 × 1.4 = 420 kg; 420 ÷ 50 = 8.4, so 9 bags. Using 300 ÷ 50 = 6 forgets the area.
workedSolution: 1. 300 × 1.4 = 420 kg; 420 ÷ 50 = 8.4, so 9 bags. Using 300 ÷ 50 = 6 forgets the area.

stem: Groundnuts are planted in rows 45 cm apart with one plant every 7.5 cm. Calculate the plant population per hectare, to the nearest whole plant.
Tatenda shelled 1,500 kg of dry groundnut pods and obtained 1,080 kg of kernels. Calculate the shelling percentage.
explanation: 1,080 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 72%. Dividing the pod mass by the kernel mass gives more than 100%, which is impossible.
workedSolution: 1. 1,080 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 72%. Dividing the pod mass by the kernel mass gives more than 100%, which is impossible.

stem: Farai will plant 3 ha of soya at 80 kg/ha. Assume one sachet of inoculant treats 50 kg of seed. How many sachets must he buy? Round UP.
explanation: Seed = 80 × 3 = 240 kg; 240 ÷ 50 = 4.8, so 5 sachets. Rounding down leaves some seed uninoculated.
workedSolution:
1. Seed = 80 × 3 = 240 kg.
2. Sachets = 240 ÷ 50 = 4.8.
3. Round up: 5 sachets.

stem: Name the poison produced by moulds growing on damp groundnuts.
explanation: **Aflatoxin**, produced by *Aspergillus* moulds.

stem: Explain **two** benefits of growing a legume before maize in a rotation.

points.description: Legumes fix atmospheric nitrogen through Rhizobium in root nodules.
Residues release this nitrogen as they decompose, so the maize needs less nitrogen fertiliser.
The legume belongs to a different family, so maize pests and diseases have no host for a season.
So their numbers fall and the maize suffers less damage (also: deep roots / residues improve soil structure).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The legume fixes nitrogen through Rhizobium in its nodules, and the residues release it to the next maize crop, which then needs less top dressing. Because it is a different family, maize pests and diseases such as grey leaf spot die out for a season, so the maize is healthier.

explanation: Nitrogen and break-crop benefits.
hints: Think of nitrogen and of pests and diseases.

stem: Describe how Sipho should inoculate and plant soya bean seed on land where soya has never been grown.

points.description: Use fresh inoculant of the correct type for soya, stored cool and within its expiry date.
Mix it with the seed (with a little water or sticker) in the shade, not in direct sun.
Do not mix inoculated seed with fertiliser or incompatible seed dressings.
Plant into moist soil the same day and cover the seed promptly.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Sipho should buy fresh soya inoculant and keep it cool. In the shade he dampens the seed slightly and mixes in the inoculant so every seed is coated, keeping it away from fertiliser and seed dressings. He plants into moist soil the same day and covers the seed at once.

explanation: Correct strain, shade, no fertiliser contact, plant at once.
hints: Keep the bacteria alive and in contact with the seed.

stem:
Pupils at a school near Chipinge tested gypsum on groundnuts using two 100 m² plots.

| Treatment | Dry pods from the 100 m² plot (kg) | Empty pods (pops) in a sample of 100 pods |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Without gypsum | 21 | 30 |
| With gypsum at early flowering | 28 | 8 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the yield of dry pods from the gypsum plot in t/ha.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in pod yield due to gypsum, to the nearest whole number.
parts.explanation: (28 − 21) ÷ 21 × 100 = 33.3%, about 33%. Dividing by 28 gives 25%, which is wrong.
parts.workedSolution: 1. (28 − 21) ÷ 21 × 100 = 33.3%, about 33%. Dividing by 28 gives 25%, which is wrong.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the nutrient in gypsum that reduced the number of empty pods.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain how the gypsum reduced the number of empty pods.

points.description: Gypsum supplies soluble calcium to the pegging zone.
Developing pods absorb calcium directly from the soil around them (not from the roots).
With enough calcium the kernels fill properly, so fewer pods are empty (pops).

explanation: Calculate yield and increase from a gypsum trial and explain the role of calcium.

stem:
A farmer near Bindura compared inoculated and uninoculated soya beans on new land.

| Treatment | Mean number of nodules per plant | Grain yield (t/ha) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Not inoculated | 2 | 1.40 |
| Inoculated | 31 | 2.45 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in yield due to inoculation.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Why did the uninoculated plants have so few nodules?

options.content: Soya plants never form any nodules unless fertiliser is added
options.rationale: Nodules form when the right bacteria are present.

options.content: The plants were too young to have roots
options.rationale: Both sets of plants grew the same time.

options.content: The correct bacteria were not present in the new land
options.rationale: Correct: soya needs its own specific bacteria.

options.content: Nodules only form on cereal crops
options.rationale: Nodules form on legumes.

parts.explanation: Specific bacteria for soya are usually absent where soya has not been grown before.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain how the extra nodules increased the yield.

points.description: Rhizobium in the nodules fixes nitrogen gas from the soil air.
It is converted to ammonium compounds supplied to the plant (the plant gives the bacteria sugars).
More nitrogen allows more protein and chlorophyll, so more leaf growth, photosynthesis and pods/seed.
Store it cool and use before the expiry date.
Mix with seed in the shade, out of direct sunlight.
Plant the same day and keep it away from fertiliser and incompatible seed dressings.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Suggest why inoculation is a cheap way to increase soya yields compared with applying nitrogen fertiliser.

points.description: A sachet of inoculant costs far less than the nitrogen fertiliser that would supply the same nitrogen.
Fixed nitrogen is not leached like fertiliser and also benefits the next crop.

explanation: Interpret an inoculation trial and explain nitrogen fixation and the handling of inoculant.
hints: Link nodules to nitrogen and to yield.
Inoculant is cheap compared with nitrogen fertiliser.

stem: Thandeka's Spanish-type groundnuts near Mutoko show yellowing leaves in April, and some kernels in a pulled plant are well coloured. Heavy rain is forecast.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: State **two** signs that would confirm the crop is ready to lift.

points.description: Most pods show a darkened inside of the shell.
Kernels have well-coloured skins / leaves yellowing and dropping.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain why delaying the harvest is risky for this type of groundnut.

points.description: Spanish types have little seed dormancy.
So mature kernels may sprout in the moist soil, and pods left in the ground also rot or detach.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Describe how she should dry the lifted plants.

points.description: Shake off soil and lay plants in windrows with the pods upwards, off damp ground.
Then stack them loosely (in stooks) in the open until the pods rattle, before picking.

parts.explanation: Pods up, off the soil, airy.

explanation: Maturity, harvest timing and drying of groundnuts.
hints: Spanish types have little seed dormancy.
